question: If we've got a weapon logged as evidence, can we tell who it was taken off and what happened to them?
expected_answer: Yes. For example, the 30-bore pistol logged as evidence in FIR 891/24 was recovered from شہزیب عرف شابی, whose recorded status on that case is 'گرفتار، بعد ازاں سزا یافتہ' (arrested, later convicted). The trail runs from the weapon entry to the FIR number to the accused named on that FIR — though it relies on matching the FIR number rather than an enforced database key.
actual_answer:
Yes — for 30 of the 32 weapons logged as evidence, the register records who the weapon was recovered from, and that person's status on the same case can be read directly from the record.

For example:
- A 30 بور پستول, بغیر لائسنس was logged in FIR 891/24 and recovered from شہزیب عرف شابی. The recorded status on that case is گرفتار، بعد ازاں سزا یافتہ. The criminal-record system also records "Convicted, on bail pending appeal" for that person on the same FIR.

This same chain applies to 11 other weapons:
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 3 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 214/26; recovered from شہزیب عرف شابی; recorded status on that case: گرفتار. The criminal-record system also records "Under trial" for that person on the same FIR.
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 6 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 1001/26; recovered from کاشف; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 6 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 201/26; recovered from فیصل; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 6 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 202/26; recovered from طارق; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 203/26; recovered from ندیم; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 6 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 204/26; recovered from کاشف; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 3 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 210/26; recovered from ذیشان; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 3 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 212/26; recovered from عمران; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 213/26; recovered from کاشف; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 217/26; recovered from کاشف; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.
- 30 بور پستول بمعہ 3 گولیاں, بغیر لائسنس — logged in FIR 218/26; recovered from عدنان; recorded status on that case: زیر تفتیش.

However, 2 of the 32 weapons record no person at all — they are crime-scene recoveries rather than items taken off an accused:
- عام لکڑی کی چھڑی، ایک عدد (fir-117-26)
- خالی خول (فائرنگ کا شاہد)، جائے وقوعہ سے برآمد (fir-266-26)

Caveat: The weapon -> person link is NOT an enforced database key. The weapon register stores `recovered_from` as a bare name, so it is matched to the accused named in the SAME FIR — i.e., the trail runs weapon -> FIR number -> accused. The criminal-record outcome above is joined the same way, on the FIR number parsed out of a free-text case reference. It holds for this data, but a name repeated across two FIRs would not be distinguished by it [Document 1].

question: جب کوئی شخص تھانے آ کر شکایت درج کراتا ہے، تو کیا وہ کسی باقاعدہ ایف آئی آر سے منسلک ہو جاتی ہے، یا دونوں الگ الگ ہی رہتے ہیں؟

question: Kya wusee criminal-history records mein koi aisa shakhs hai jo hamare apne darj kiye hue kisi case se match nahi karta?
expected_answer: Haan, ek — Waqas (00000-9000020-1) — criminal records system mein mojood hai magar iska koi matching local FIR-accused record nahi. Tawaqqo yehi hai: woh system ek beruni/wifaqi record source ki numainda hai, sirf local FIRs ka aks nahi.
actual_answer:
Yes, there is exactly one person in the criminal-records system who does not have a matching accused record in any of the FIRs we have registered:
  - وقاص (CNIC 00000-9000020-1) — criminal record(s) criminal_record:CR-C106-1; the same NAME does appear among our accused, but on a different CNIC, so this is not a spelling mismatch.

This result is based on a comparison of 33 criminal records covering 32 distinct people, against 94 accused entries across our FIRs (92 distinct CNICs). Matching was done on CNIC, not on name.

This is expected rather than a data-quality defect. The criminal-records system is an external/federal record source, not a mirror of our FIRs, so it can legitimately hold someone we have never charged. 31 of 32 subjects DO match a local accused record, so this is a single outlier, not a systematic linkage failure [Document 1].

question: What kinds of cases are we dealing with now compared to a couple of years back?
expected_answer: 2024 (13 FIRs) is a single narrow pattern — every case is armed robbery (PPC 34, 392, Arms Ordinance §13, each 13/13). 2026 (51 FIRs) is far more diversified: the armed-robbery cluster persists (34 x23, 392 x8, Arms Ord x16) alongside narcotics (CNSA §9(c) x12), cyber fraud/harassment (PECA §14 & §21, x9 each), financial fraud (419/420, x9 each), kidnapping (365-A x5), murder (302 x8), domestic violence (x4). Overall the armed-robbery baseline persists, but the mix has broadened substantially toward cyber-enabled and financial crime.
actual_answer:
Compared to 2024, the number of FIRs (First Information Reports) has increased significantly in 2026, from 13 to 51. In 2024, all the FIRs were related to legal acts under the **Pakistan Penal Code (PPC)** and the **Arms Ordinance 1965**, specifically citing **PPC §34**, **PPC §392**, and **Arms Ordinance 1965 §13**.

In 2026, the range of legal acts charged has expanded. While **PPC** and **Arms Ordinance 1965** are still heavily involved, additional legal acts such as the **Control of Narcotic Substances Act 1997 (CNSA 1997)**, **Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 (PECA 2016)**, **Punjab Domestic Violence Act**, and **Illegal Dispossession Act 2005** are now also being cited. 

Specific sections charged in 2026 include a broader range of provisions, such as **PPC §34**, **Arms Ordinance 1965 §13**, **CNSA 1997 §9(c)**, **PECA 2016 §§14 and 21**, **PPC §§337-A(i), 419, 420, 302, 392, 506, 365-A, 384**, **Punjab Domestic Violence Act**, and **Illegal Dispossession Act 2005 §3**.

This indicates a diversification in the types of cases being reported and charged over time, with an increase in the number of FIRs and the inclusion of more legal acts and specific sections in 2026 compared to 2024 [Document 1].

question: Is caseload growing faster at our general-purpose stations, or at the handful set up for one specific type of crime?

actual_answer: The caseload is growing faster at the general-purpose stations. Specifically, the 15 general-purpose stations saw an increase from 7 FIRs in 2024 to 39 FIRs in 2026. In contrast, the 2 stations set up for one specific type of crime saw a much slower increase, from 3 FIRs in 2024 to 5 FIRs in 2026 [Document 1].

question: ایک طرف یہ دیکھیں کہ لوگوں پر کن دفعات میں مقدمے بن رہے ہیں، اور دوسری طرف یہ کہ وہ مقدمے عدالت میں کہاں تک پہنچے — کیا دونوں سے کیس لوڈ کی سنگینی کا ایک ہی اندازہ ہوتا ہے؟
expected_answer: نہیں — دونوں ایک دوسرے سے پیچھے ہیں۔ ایف آئی آر کی دفعات پہلے ہی ظاہر کرتی ہیں کہ سنگین جرائم عام ہیں، لیکن 33 میں سے صرف 1 کرمنل ریکارڈ حتمی سزا ہے؛ 30 اب بھی زیرِ سماعت ہیں۔ موجودہ کیس لوڈ کی سنگینی کا اندازہ ایف آئی آر/دفعات کی گنتی پر لگانا چاہیے، سزاؤں کی گنتی پر نہیں، جو ابھی پیچھے ہے۔
actual_answer:
No, the two perspectives do not give the same impression of the severity of the caseload. 

On one side, 73 cases are being charged under various FIR sections, with the most common being PPC §34 (40 cases), Arms Ordinance 1965 §13 (29 cases), and PPC §392 (21 cases). These figures reflect the full scope of charges currently being brought against individuals.

On the other side, only 1 out of 33 criminal records has reached a verdict, while the rest are still in progress. This means that the conviction count only reflects 3% of the recorded court caseload, and thus lags significantly behind the number of charges being filed.

Therefore, the severity of the current caseload should be understood based on the FIR/section counts, as the conviction counts do not provide a complete or up-to-date picture [Document 1].

question: ہتھیار عام طور پر کس نوعیت کے مقدمات میں سامنے آتے ہیں، اور کیا 2024 کے مقابلے میں اب یہ نوعیت بدل گئی ہے؟

question: Acting as a crime analyst, review our current caseload and flag anything that looks unusual or worth monitoring.
expected_answer: Approach: profile the accused, the victims, the property and the timing across the 73 FIRs, and flag what doesn't look routine. What stands out: (1) the offender profile is unusually uniform — every accused is between 24 and 49 (average ~31), none younger or older; (2) where an accused–complainant relationship is recorded at all, 'stranger' dominates, so this is largely stranger-perpetrated crime rather than disputes between people who know each other, apart from the domestic-violence cases; (3) seized-property records point to more fatalities than the charge sheet alone — 13 items sent to a forensic lab and 7 held for return to a deceased's heirs, alongside 8 murder-section FIRs; (4) incident times are fairly flat across the day with only a mild evening lean, so there's no strong night-crime pattern to build a patrol case around. The uniform offender profile and the stranger-perpetrated skew are the most useful things to keep watching.
actual_answer:
Based on the current caseload, several patterns and anomalies stand out that warrant further monitoring:

- The age range and average age of the accused are based on a minority of the total accused individuals. Specifically, only 17 of the 92 accused have recorded ages, with ages ranging from 24 to 49 and an average age of 31.5 [Document 1]. This limited data coverage suggests that the age profile of the majority of accused individuals remains unknown, which could be significant for understanding the demographic trends of criminal activity.

- The most frequently recorded relationship between the accused and the complainant is "اجنبی (stranger)," which appears in 15 of the 24 relationship entries and is documented in 6 FIRs [Document 2]. This suggests that a significant portion of incidents involve individuals who are not personally known to the complainant, which may indicate a pattern of random or opportunistic crimes.

- In cases involving seized property, 28 FIRs record seized items, with a total of 45 items across these cases. Of these, 13 items were sent to a forensic laboratory, and 7 items were held for return to the deceased person's heirs [Document 3]. This indicates that a portion of the seized property is being processed for forensic analysis, which may be relevant for ongoing investigations or evidence collection.

- The distribution of incidents by time of day shows that the busiest time is the evening (18:00-23:59), with 19 incidents recorded [Document 4]. This suggests that a significant number of incidents occur during the evening hours, which may be worth monitoring for patterns or potential hotspots.

- Certain accused individuals appear in more than one FIR. Specifically, **فیصل** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 401/26 and FIR 202/26. **طارق** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 401/26 and FIR 202/26. **شہزیب عرف شابی** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 891/24 and FIR 214/26. **عاصم رشید** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 64/26 and FIR 65/26 [Document 5]. question: What legal requirement governs how a report of a crime becomes a formal FIR, and does our recordkeeping actually follow it?
expected_answer: Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 requires that oral information about a cognizable offence given to the officer-in-charge of a police station be reduced to writing, read back to the informant, signed by them, and entered in a register in the prescribed form — that's the actual legal basis for what we call an FIR. Our FIR records follow that structure in outline but not completely: all 73 cases carry complainant details, 70 of 73 carry a recording officer, and only 64 of 73 carry a report timestamp. ### Legal Requirement:
The legal requirement governing how a report of a crime becomes a formal FIR is outlined in **Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure**, as referenced in **Document 2**. According to this provision, every information relating to an offence, whether cognizable or non-cognizable, must be recorded in writing by the officer in charge of a police station. Furthermore, the substance of the information must be entered in the police station daily diary, which is the book provided for the purpose.

### Recordkeeping Compliance:
Our recordkeeping follows the structure outlined in **Document 7**, which provides a summary of our own case records. According to this summary:
- **Complainant details** are recorded in **73 of 73 cases**.

- **The time the report was made** is recorded in **73 of 73 cases**.

question: Why doesn't our system keep a record of what a witness or an accused person actually said in a police interview — is that a data gap?
expected_answer: No, that's by design, not a gap. Under the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, Article 38, a confession made to a police officer cannot be used as evidence against the accused, and Article 39 extends that to confessions made while in police custody unless made in the immediate presence of a magistrate. Separately, Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 bars a police-recorded statement from being used at trial except for narrow, court-controlled purposes. Because none of that content is legally usable evidence while it's in police hands, our witness records only store identity and contact details of each witness — name, CNIC, address, relationship to the complainant — and there is no field anywhere in the system for confession or interview-statement text. That's consistent with how the law scopes what a police record is meant to hold.

According to the provided documents, statements made by a person to a police officer during an investigation can be reduced into writing, but they do not have to be signed by the person making the statement. question: Does the law expect the officer who first registers a case to be the same one who investigates it, or are those meant to be separate roles — and does that match what actually happens in our data?
expected_answer: The law expects separation. Article 18 of the Police Order, 2002 sets up a distinct Investigation Wing under a dedicated head of investigation, states that registered cases "shall be investigated by the investigation staff" under that head, and bars the District Police Officer from interfering in the investigation process — the clear intent is that logging a case and investigating it are separate functions. In practice, our data shows the opposite: the officer who records the FIR and the officer who ends up investigating it are the same person in 68 of 74 pairs (92%); role-splitting happens in only 6 cases. So the separation the law sets up isn't what's actually happening on the ground in this data.

### Part 1: What the Law Requires

The law does not explicitly require the officer who first registers a case to be the same one who investigates it. Instead, it allows for flexibility in assigning these roles. For example, under **Section 156 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Pakistan)**, any officer in charge of a police station may investigate a cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate [Document 2]. Furthermore, **Section 157(1)** of the same code allows the officer in charge to depute a subordinate to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case [Document 6]. This implies that the roles of registering and investigating a case can be performed by different officers.

### Part 2: What Actually Happens in Our Data

According to the summary of our own case records [Document 7], the roles of the officer who recorded the FIR and the officer who investigated the case are **mostly not separated**. In **68 out of 74 recorded assignment pairs (92%)**, the same officer both recorded the FIR and conducted the investigation. The roles are split in only **6 cases**, and in **3 of those 6**, the investigating officer had no recording officer on the same case at all, making the pair unresolvable rather than genuinely split. This indicates that, in practice, the same officer is often responsible for both registering and investigating a case, which aligns with the legal provisions that allow for such overlap.

question: What kinds of cases are we dealing with now compared to a couple of years back?
expected_answer: 2024 (13 FIRs) is a single narrow pattern — every case is armed robbery (PPC 34, 392, Arms Ordinance §13, each 13/13). 2026 (51 FIRs) is far more diversified: the armed-robbery cluster persists (34 x23, 392 x8, Arms Ord x16) alongside narcotics (CNSA §9(c) x12), cyber fraud/harassment (PECA §14 & §21, x9 each), financial fraud (419/420, x9 each), kidnapping (365-A x5), murder (302 x8), domestic violence (x4). Overall the armed-robbery baseline persists, but the mix has broadened substantially toward cyber-enabled and financial crime.
actual_answer:
Compared to 2024, in 2026 there has been a significant increase in the number of FIRs, from 13 to 51. In 2024, all cases were charged under the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) and the Arms Ordinance 1965, specifically under sections 34 and 392 of the PPC and section 13 of the Arms Ordinance 1965 [Document 1].

In 2026, the legal acts charged are more diverse. While the PPC still plays a major role (39 FIRs), other legal acts such as the Control of Narcotic Substances Act 1997 (CNSA 1997), the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 (PECA 2016), the Punjab Domestic Violence Act, and the Illegal Dispossession Act 2005 are also involved. The specific sections charged in 2026 include a broader range, such as PPC §34, Arms Ordinance 1965 §13, CNSA 1997 §9(c), PECA 2016 §§14 and 21, and others. This indicates a shift towards more varied and complex legal issues being addressed in FIRs compared to 2024 [Document 1].

question: Is caseload growing faster at our general-purpose stations, or at the handful set up for one specific type of crime?

question: ایک طرف یہ دیکھیں کہ لوگوں پر کن دفعات میں مقدمے بن رہے ہیں، اور دوسری طرف یہ کہ وہ مقدمے عدالت میں کہاں تک پہنچے — کیا دونوں سے کیس لوڈ کی سنگینی کا ایک ہی اندازہ ہوتا ہے؟
expected_answer: نہیں — دونوں ایک دوسرے سے پیچھے ہیں۔ ایف آئی آر کی دفعات پہلے ہی ظاہر کرتی ہیں کہ سنگین جرائم عام ہیں، لیکن 33 میں سے صرف 1 کرمنل ریکارڈ حتمی سزا ہے؛ 30 اب بھی زیرِ سماعت ہیں۔ موجودہ کیس لوڈ کی سنگینی کا اندازہ ایف آئی آر/دفعات کی گنتی پر لگانا چاہیے، سزاؤں کی گنتی پر نہیں، جو ابھی پیچھے ہے۔
actual_answer:
No, the two perspectives do not give the same impression of the severity of the case load. 

On one side, 73 cases are being charged under various statutes, with the most frequent being PPC §34 (40 cases), Arms Ordinance 1965 §13 (29 cases), and PPC §392 (21 cases). This shows the range and frequency of charges being brought.

On the other side, out of 33 criminal records, only 1 has reached a verdict, while the rest are still in progress. The status of these cases includes "Under trial" (30 cases), "Convicted, on bail pending appeal" (1 case), "Sub judice, external prior case" (1 case), and "Under trial, priority hearing requested" (1 case). The only case that has reached a verdict is FIR 891-24 (شہزیب عرف شابی), which was convicted under PPC §392 and is on bail pending appeal.

Therefore, while the FIR/section counts provide a comprehensive view of the current case load and the charges being brought, the conviction counts lag significantly behind, reflecting only a small portion (3%) of the recorded court caseload. As a result, the severity of the current case load should be assessed based on the FIR/section counts, not the conviction counts [Document 1].

question: ہتھیار عام طور پر کس نوعیت کے مقدمات میں سامنے آتے ہیں، اور کیا 2024 کے مقابلے میں اب یہ نوعیت بدل گئی ہے؟

In 2026, the weapon charges were still associated with PPC §34 and PPC §392, but also appeared alongside CNSA 1997 §9(c) and PPC §302, which were not associated with weapons charges in 2024. question: Kya log 2026 mein waqiaat ki police ko itni hi jaldi ittila de rahe hain jitni 2024 mein dete the?

question: Acting as a crime analyst, review our current caseload and flag anything that looks unusual or worth monitoring.
expected_answer: Approach: profile the accused, the victims, the property and the timing across the 73 FIRs, and flag what doesn't look routine. What stands out: (1) the offender profile is unusually uniform — every accused is between 24 and 49 (average ~31), none younger or older; (2) where an accused–complainant relationship is recorded at all, 'stranger' dominates, so this is largely stranger-perpetrated crime rather than disputes between people who know each other, apart from the domestic-violence cases; (3) seized-property records point to more fatalities than the charge sheet alone — 13 items sent to a forensic lab and 7 held for return to a deceased's heirs, alongside 8 murder-section FIRs; (4) incident times are fairly flat across the day with only a mild evening lean, so there's no strong night-crime pattern to build a patrol case around. The uniform offender profile and the stranger-perpetrated skew are the most useful things to keep watching.
actual_answer:
Based on the current caseload, several patterns and anomalies stand out that warrant further monitoring:

- The age range and average age of the accused are only based on a minority of the records. Specifically, out of 92 distinct accused individuals, only 17 have recorded ages, ranging from 24 to 49, with an average age of 31.5. The remaining 75 accused have no recorded age, which limits the reliability of any broader demographic profiling [Document 1].

- The relationship between the accused and the complainant is most commonly recorded as "اجنبی (stranger)," appearing in 15 of the 24 recorded relationships across 10 FIRs. This relationship is found in 6 FIRs, suggesting that a significant portion of incidents involve individuals who are not known to the complainant [Document 2].

- Seized property is recorded in 28 FIRs, with a total of 45 property-register entries. Of these, 13 items were sent to a forensic laboratory, and 7 items are held for return to the deceased person's heirs. This indicates that a portion of the seized items are being processed for forensic analysis, while others are being managed for legal or familial return [Document 3].

- The timing of incidents is unevenly distributed. Out of 64 incidents with recorded time, the busiest time of day is evening (18:00-23:59), with 19 incidents. Morning (06:00-11:59) and afternoon (12:00-17:59) each account for 14 and 16 incidents, respectively, while night (00:00-05:59) accounts for only 1 incident. Additionally, 14 of the 64 incidents record exactly 00:00:00, which is a placeholder for a date with no clock time rather than a real midnight [Document 4].

- Certain accused individuals appear in more than one FIR. Specifically:

  - **فیصل** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 401/26 and FIR 202/26.
  - **طارق** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 401/26 and FIR 202/26.
  - **شہزیب عرف شابی** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 891/24 and FIR 214/26.
  - **عاصم رشید** appears in **2 cases**: FIR 64/26 and FIR 65/26.

These findings suggest that while some patterns are emerging, the data is incomplete in several areas, particularly regarding the age of the accused and the exact timing of incidents. The presence of recurring accused individuals across multiple FIRs also indicates potential links between cases that may require further investigation.

question: فرض کریں آپ کسی ایس ایچ او کو بریفنگ دے رہے ہیں کہ کون سے مقدمے دب کر یا نظر سے اوجھل ہو کر رہ سکتے ہیں — آپ کن چیزوں کی نشاندہی کریں گے؟
expected_answer: طریقہ کار: ایسے مقدمات تلاش کریں جن کے اپنے ریکارڈ اتنے مربوط نہیں کہ اُن پر انحصار کیا جا سکے۔ قابلِ توجہ نکات: (1) 9 ایف آئی آر میں واقعے کی تاریخ درج نہیں اور زیادہ تر روزنامچہ (زمنی) اندراجات کی کوئی قسم درج نہیں، اس لیے اِن مقدمات میں یہ واضح طور پر ترتیب دینا ممکن نہیں کہ کیا کب ہوا؛ (2) 73 میں سے 13 ایف آئی آر میں افسر کے تھانے سے جائے وقوعہ کی طرف روانگی کا وقت خود رپورٹ کے وقت سے پہلے کا درج ہے — یہ ترتیب کا تضاد ہے جو جانچ میں نہیں ٹکے گا؛ (3) واک اِن شکایات اور ایف آئی آر الگ الگ نظاموں میں ہیں جو صرف ایک اختیاری مشترکہ ٹیگ سے جُڑے ہیں، اس لیے غلط یا غائب ٹیگ والی شکایت ایف آئی آر موجود ہونے کے باوجود بغیر کارروائی کے دکھائی دے سکتی ہے۔ اِن میں سے کوئی بھی اکیلے کسی مقدمے کو ضائع نہیں کرتی، لیکن ہر ایک وہ خلا ہے جو جائزے میں رکاوٹ بنتا ہے۔
actual_answer:
When briefing an SHO about cases that may be stalled or overlooked, the following key issues should be highlighted, based on the cross-case aggregate data [Document 1]:

1. **Missing Incident Dates in FIRs**: Nine FIRs (fir-205-26, fir-211-26, fir-340-25, fir-406-26, fir-410-25, fir-422-26, fir-457-26, fir-467-26, fir-77-26) do not record an incident date. This lack of information makes it impossible to establish a reliable timeline for these cases.

2. **Unclear Investigation Status**: Fifty-two of the 73 FIRs do not have a recorded investigation status. This makes it impossible to track the progress of these cases, and they may quietly stall without anyone noticing.

3. **Missing Entry Types in Roznamcha/Zimni Diary Entries**: Out of 259 roznamcha/zimni diary entries, 188 (approximately 73%) do not record the entry type. This omission makes it difficult to determine the sequence of events or the nature of each investigative step within a case.

4. **Chronological Contradictions in FIRs**: Thirteen FIRs (fir-118-26, fir-203-26, fir-301-26, fir-403-26, fir-407-26, fir-413-26, fir-423-26, fir-424-26, fir-434-26, fir-449-26, fir-458-26, fir-468-26, and others) record the officer's departure from the station as earlier than the report time. This contradiction could be problematic in court. Additionally, only 44 of the 73 FIRs record a departure time at all.

5. **Disconnection Between Walk-in Complaints and FIRs**: Walk-in complaints and FIRs are stored in separate systems and are only linked by an optional shared tag (CMS.case_tag_number = FIR.e_tag_number), which is not enforced by any database key. This can lead to complaints appearing unactioned even when a corresponding FIR exists, especially if the tag is mistyped or missing. However, four of the four complaints currently resolve to a real FIR.

question: آپ عدالت کو حوالگی کے لیے ایک کیس فائل تیار کر رہے ہیں — ڈیٹا کی روشنی میں، کن چیزوں کے نامکمل قرار پانے کا سب سے زیادہ امکان ہے؟

actual_answer:
When preparing a case file for court, the following items are most likely to be incomplete based on the data:

question: Baramad shuda hathiyaron ki record keeping ko dekhte hue, kya koi aisi baat hai jo compliance ke lihaz se flag karne layak ho?
expected_answer: Tareeqa: 32 weapon-register entries ka jaiza lein — license status, case aur shakhs se rabta, aur handling record ki takmeel. Bila-license ki shrah sab se numaya point hai.
actual_answer:
Reviewing the 32 weapon-register entries for compliance:

This is a gap in the form, not in one officer's paperwork.
  - Weapons attach to a case only by a SOFT match on the FIR code written into the register — plain text, no enforced key. All 32 resolve to a real case today, but a single mistyped code would silently orphan an item with nothing raising an error.

question: Yahan naye tainaat hone wale afsar ke liye ek mukhtasar orientation note likhein — unhein mojooda case load se kya tawaqqo rakhni chahiye?
expected_answer: Aap 9 zilon mein phaili 73 khuli FIRs sambhaal rahe hain, zyada bojh Faisalabad aur Lahore mein. Case load haal hi mein badla hai: do saal pehle taqreeban sab kuch armed robbery tha; ab manshiyat, cyber fraud aur online haraasgi, mali fraud, aghwa aur qatal ka mishra hai, jisme armed robbery ab bhi sab se bara silsila hai.
